etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 手(て)洗(あら)い (tearai, “hand washing”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) + 茶 (cha, “tea”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *saki. Cognate with 崎(さき) (saki, “peninsula, cape”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 先 (MC sen|senH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle Chinese 全部 (dzjwen buX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 始(はじ)めて (hajimete), the conjunctive form of the verb 始(はじ)める (hajimeru, “to begin, to start”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from 初(はじ)めて (hajimete) above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Chinese 醫者 /医者 (yīzhě).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: May originally have been an onomatopoeia. Compare ふうふう (fūfū, “to blow with one's lips rounded”) .

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 學生 (MC haewk sraeng). The use of the 呉音 (go'on, literally “Wu sound”) reading for the first character and the 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”) reading for the second character suggests either an innovation within Japanese, or later influence from another dialect of Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨omo₂pu⟩ → */əməpu/ → /omoɸu/ → /omou/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *əməp-. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Also appears in the Man'yōshū poetry compilation, completed c. 759 CE. There are two main theories for its ultimate derivation:
* May be cognate with 面 (omo, “face”), from the sense of how one's emotions appear on one's face.
* May be cognate with 重 (omo, “weight”), from the sense of weighing different options. Compare similar derivations of English ponder (as in “to weigh; to think”) and ponderous (as in “heavy, weighty”). However, this runs into problems, since the ancestor of this form is reconstructed as *onpo- (“heavy”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 下二段 (shimo nidan) verb 捨つ (sutsu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 捨つ entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/paru/ → /ɸaru/ → /haru/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 春 (MC tsyhwin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 曇(くも)る (kumoru, “to become cloudy, to cloud up”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kaku (“to scratch”).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Cognate with 掻く (kaku, “to scratch”) (letters were originally scratched or carved into wood in order to write); compare English write, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan (“to scratch, carve”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 来 (rai-, “coming..., next...”) + 月 (getsu, “month”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Simplified from 氣 (米 → 㐅) in the 1946 Tōyō kanji list.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 氣 (MC khj+jH).
The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Mandarin 氣 /气 (qi), Northern Min 氣 /气 (ki̿), Min Nan 氣 /气 (khì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 氣 (MC khj+jH).
The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare Eastern Min 氣 /气 (ké).
In Old Japanese, this kanji is used to transcribe the 借音 (shakuon) kana of ⟨ke₂⟩.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/manɡwa/ → /manɡa/
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese‐derived elements, as a compound of 漫(まん) (man, “as one pleases”) + 画(が) (ga, “picture”).
The sense of a drawing first appears in 1798 in the foreword to Santō Kyōden's picture book 四(し)時(じの)交(ゆき)加(かい) (Shiji no Yukikai), already using the modern shinjitai spelling of 漫画.
The archaic sense of “Eurasian spoonbill” is attested even earlier in the 1778 medical text 薬(やく)品(ひん)手(て)引(びき)草(ぐさ) (Yakuhin Tebikigusa).
In the late nineteenth century, the term was repurposed as a translation for the English word caricature. This shift was led by artists such as Imaizumi Ippyō and Kitazawa Rakuten to elevate satirical drawings (formerly known as ポンチ絵(え) (ponchi-e)) into a professional art form. It later expanded to encompass sequential “comics” as that medium gained popularity in the early twentieth century.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 熱 (MC nyet).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 用 (MC yowngH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 紙, cited to manuscript kana glosses in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kanpi (the modern standard Japanese form results from a sporadic change of [ᵐb] to [m]). Cognate with Okinawan 紙 (kabi). Compare also Ainu カㇺピ (kampi, “paper”), from Proto-Ainu *kanpi (which is assumed to have been borrowed from Japonic).
An alternative hypothesis explains the Old Japanese word as a borrowing from Middle Chinese 簡 (kean^X, “bamboo slip used for writing”), with a shift in pronunciation from kan → */kamu/ → /kami/, with excrescent final -i as in 文 (fumi) from borrowed bun or pun. That would require the forms based on [ᵐb] to result from the sporadic change of [m] to [ᵐb], as in 黍 (/⁠kibi⁠/, “millet”) from Old Japanese 寸三 (/⁠ki₁mi₁⁠/). However, Ryukyuan reflexes appear to maintain a /b/ phone, which is more difficult to explain for a borrowing from Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 紙 (MC tsyeX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese [Term?], from Proto-Japonic *kinu.
Possibly cognate with Chinese 絹 /绢 (juàn, “silk”) (compare Middle Chinese 絹 (kjwienH)) via early borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/omo₂pu/ → /omwopoju/ → /omwoɸoju/ → /omoɸoju/ → /oboɸoju/ → /oboju/ → /obojuru/ → /obojeru/ → /oboeru/
Ultimately from Old Japanese verb 思(おも)ふ (omopu, modern 思(おも)う (omou, “to think (about or of something)”)). The historical derivation is roughly as follows:
* the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) omopa of Old Japanese verb 思(おも)ふ (omopu, “to think”, modern 思(おも)う (omou)) + ゆ (-yu, Old Japanese verb suffix denoting intransitive, spontaneous, or passive action):
: omopayu → omopoyu
: The 思ほゆ (omopoyu) form is found in the Nihon Shoki and the Man'yōshū.
* contraction and regular sound changes:
: omopoyu → omofoyu → obowoyu → oboyu
: This change is already evident by the early Heian period.
* regular historical grammatical shifts occurring for classical 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs:
: oboyu → oboyuru → oboyeru → oboeru
: This set of shifts occurred during the Kamakura and Muromachi periods.
The verb was originally used in intransitive and passive contexts, in accordance with its derivation. It began to be used in more active and transitive contexts starting from roughly the mid-Heian period, with the learn and memorize senses appearing in the Kamakura period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The seemingly unrelated senses "to investigate" and "to play an instrument" are probably a semantic loan from Middle Chinese 調 (MC dewH) via kanbun kundoku.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 質問 (MC tsyit mjunH, literally “quality + ask”), apparently borrowed later as a learned borrowing from Literary Chinese of the same source term.
First attested in 1771.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 起く (oku), in the 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *əku.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.
First cited to the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pen/ → /fen/ → /hen/
From Middle Chinese 邊 (MC pen, “edge; margin, border; nearby, vicinity”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pe₁/ → /pe/ → /fe/ → /he/
From Old Japanese. The root of the modern Japanese directional particle へ (e).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/pe₁/ → /pe/ → /be/
From Old Japanese, from pe above. The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 辺 (he, “vicinity”, see he above) + た (ta, “place, area”, the same ta element in 貴方 anata, now “you” in modern Japanese but previously meaning “that one over there”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From at least the late Heian period. Originally a compound of 辺 (he, “vicinity”, see he above) + ち (chi, “area?”, the same chi element used to indicate general area in こち kochi, “around here, this area” and related words).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be a compound of な (na, alternative form of の no, the possessive particle) + 辺 (be, “vicinity”, see be above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 郵便(ゆうびん) (yūbin, “postal service”) + 局(きょく) (-kyoku, “office”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From おもき (omoki), the 連体形 (rentaikei, “attributive form”) of Early Middle Japanese adjective 重し (omoshi), with the medial /-k-/ falling out; eventually from Proto-Japonic *onpo.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 雑(ざつ) (zatsu, “miscellaneous”) + 誌(し) (shi, “record”).
Said to have been coined by Yanagawa Shunsan (柳川(やながわ)春三(しゅんさん)), publisher of 西洋(せいよう)雑誌(ざっし) (Seiyō Zasshi, “Western Magazine”, 1867), as a translation of English magazine.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sawo/ (uncertain, may be compound as opposed to root) → /awo/ → /ao/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *awo.
Appears as the latter part in older compounds with an -s- infix or prefix. It is unclear if this leading /s/ is indicative of an earlier form (sawo), or if this was an addition for euphony to avoid vowel clusters, or for other reasons. This /s/ is also seen in 雨(あめ) (ame, “rain”, becoming same in old compounds) and 稲(いね) (ine, “rice”, becoming shine in old compounds).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 青 (MC tsheng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Unknown. The reading might be an obscure term from Old Japanese or dialect. The use of the character 青 arises from its 宋音(そうおん) (sōon, “Song-dynasty pronunciation”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kuro₁⟩ → /kuro/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kuro. See also 黒(くろ)い (kuroi).
Via root morpheme *kur, cognates include:
* 涅(くり) (kuri, “black mud from the bed of a body of water”).
* 暗(くら) (kura, “darkness, deception”), 蔵(くら), 倉(くら), 庫(くら) (kura, “(dark) storehouse”), and 暗(くら)い (kurai, “dark”).
* classical verb 暮(く)る (kuru), modern 暮(く)れる (kureru, “to become dark; to near the end (of a day, year, life, etc.)”), 暗(く)れる, 眩(く)れる (kureru, “to become depressed, to become dreary of mood”), 暮(く)れ (kure, “dusk, nightfall, sunset”), and 呉(くれ) (kure, “China”, literally “land of the setting sun”).
Possibly also cognate with Ainu kur (“shadow”) and Korean 구름 (gureum, “cloud”); compare also Japanese 雲(くも) (kumo, “cloud”), Korean 검— (geom-, “black”), and Ainu kunne (“black; dark”).
